utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hello to you all. I should like to ask the registrar to call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-66-R77, the Prosecutor versus Beqa Beqaj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. I would like to inform the parties of the fact that the Trial Chamber is having this hearing with only two Judges, pursuant to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The Trial Chamber is entitled to do so in the event that one of the Judges cannot attend, and if that Judge cannot attend, the two other Judges may preside over the hearing. Therefore, the Trial Chamber is holding its session today according to Rule No. 15, Rule 15 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. That said, can you hear me well, Mr. Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you repeat that, please?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I can hear you well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Beqaj. This hearing is dedicated to the closing arguments presented by both parties. But before giving the floor to the parties, I would like to turn to the Prosecution and ask them whether they have decided which documents will be tendered into evidence under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, David Akerson on behalf of the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm informed by my case manager that we have sent a written list of what should be tendered under seal to the Registry already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to draw your attention to what was stated in the hearing which took place on the 28th of April of this year. Personally, I said, and I'm quoting my own words: "The Registrar asked me whether my [as interpreted] documents, which will be tendered must be under seal. You might want to reconsider your position and examine your position for the next hearing. Take your time, but I would like to assure you that those -- that the documents have been admitted into evidence." Would you briefly like to remind us of the documents which will be tendered under seal or may I ask the Registrar to tell us which documents are to be tendered under seal, according to the instructions provided by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, according to the Prosecution, documents Exhibit P1 has been put under seal; Exhibit P5 has been put under seal; P8 has been put under seal; P9 and P10 have respectively been put under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Does the Defence have any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. van der Spoel. I will now give the floor to Mr. Akerson. Please proceed. I would also thereby wish to draw your attention to what has been stated in Rule 86, namely the closing arguments. In paragraph 3 it is stated, "The parties shall also address matters of sentencing in closing arguments." So I am sure that you are going to be dealing with this issue also. You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. As I said, David Akerson on behalf of the Prosecution. To my left is Jason Dominguez, who is a trial attorney as well, and the case manager Sebastiaan von Hooydonk. I need to go into private session just for a moment to begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: May it please the Court and Defence counsel. Your Honours have asked counsel to discuss a number of legal matters: one is the counts in the indictment, and the second is the law on contempt. And I'm going to address those issues before moving on to an analysis of the evidence in the case. First, the indictment. There are three counts in the indictment, as you are well aware: contempt, attempt and incitement to commit attempt. And as we had stated in our pre-trial brief, the contempt charge and the attempt to commit contempt charge were charges in the alternative because the witness did, in fact, testify. It was unclear to us legally whether or not that would be construed as an attempt or actually the commission of contempt. So we would ask the Court in that case to enter a conviction, if you find that proof has been adduced beyond a reasonable doubt, to either of those, one or -- but not both, one of those counts but not both of those counts. The incitement count -- the Court had asked for a definition of incitement. The definition as it is in the dictionary is "to arouse to action or to stir up." And based on indictment and our pre-trial brief, the incitement count pertains to evidence that Beqa Beqaj, the accused, used one of the relatives of B1 in order to convey messages that B1 should withdraw his testimony. So that is the incitement count. The balance of the evidence would be pertaining to the contempt count, or the attempt count as the Court sees fit. And we would be asking that you enter a separate conviction on the incitement count, of course. As to the law of interference, Your Honour, I want to begin by drawing your attention to the first minute of this trial, my opening argument, and I began my opening argument by saying that this is a case about witness interference. And if you could turn your computers on to computer evidence now so that you could see what we are broadcasting. We are going to be showing some slides. I had indicated at the beginning of my opening argument that this is a case about interference with witnesses; not a case about threats, not a case about witness intimidation, and as such I'm going to focus my discussion on the law of interference with witnesses. The most recent case to discuss witness interference came out of the Brdjanin case which was the Maglov contempt case. And in that case the Trial Chamber defined otherwise interfering with a witness as contempt of court as requiring proof of two elements: first, that the accused is engaged in conduct that is likely to deter a witness or a potential witness from giving evidence, or engaged in conduct that is likely to influence the nature of witnesses' evidence. That's element number 1. One of those two alternatives; and the second element is that the accused acted knowingly and wilfully. Now, having studied this I think there is a loophole in this and I think there is a better construction that this Court ought to consider. The "likely to deter" I think is problematic and I want to give you an example of where I think this will cause problems, not in this case but in other cases. If you have, for example, a case where the Microsoft Corporation is being litigated and Bill Gates, who is one of the richest men in America is being sued and Bill Gates walks up to the court house and he has a witness badge on and somebody who is intent on interfering with Bill Gates approaches him and says, "I will give you 50.000 dollars if you withdraw your testimony right now." Well, Bill Gates is going to continue walking and he's going to say, "I don't need the money. It's far too small amount to money for me to even consider." And under the Maglov decision, that behaviour of that person would not be arguably considered contemptuous because it was not likely to deter Bill Gates. And I think this Court actually is going to want to regulate the behaviour of anybody who approaches a witness even if it's not likely to deter. So I think the standard here, the construction as espoused in Maglov is problematic. And I want to turn your attention to a case from England that I think is very similar to our case. It's called the Toney case, and I have some documents which I can tender to the Court. I would refer the Court to the head note on page 1 of the decision. Does Defence counsel also have a copy of this? Okay, good. In this case the appellant's brother was due to be tried on a charge of robbery and two days before trial, the appellant called to see a potential witness with whom he had been at school. The appellant spoke to the witness and told him that his brother had not been at the scene of the robbery. That was simply a factual inaccuracy and that as was all that that person did. He was charged with interfering with a witness. And that court held "the offence of perverting the course of justice by interfering with a potential witness could be committed where there is no evidence of any bribe, threat, undue pressure or other unlawful means since, notwithstanding the fact that the great majority of cases, the actus reus would be accompanied by such unlawful means and the use of unlawful means was not an essential ingredients of the offence. It followed that, since there was an ample evidence on which the jury could find that the appellant's intention was to pervert the course of justice by persuading the witness to change his evidence, the appeal would be dismissed." I would ask this Court to take a look at the definition as espoused by Maglov, because I think that a better construction would be to focus on the intent of the actor. The "likely to deter" seems to me to be focussed on the success as it's associated with the victim and if you have somebody like Bill Gates, I think you're going to have actions that would not be covered by your own contempt statute that you are going to want to have covered. And there is another thing about Maglov which -- I think there is an inconsistency, because Maglov says that you don't need to succeed in interference, and I think that conflicts with this definition, that it's likely to deter. On the one hand you don't need to succeed in your interference in order to commit contempt; but on the other hand it has to be likely to deter. So I think it's problematic. That being said, I'm going to argue Maglov for the purpose of this hearing because that is the latest definition that we have, and frankly, it's one of the only definitions of interference with witnesses, and also because in this case, it doesn't really matter because this is a case about suborning witness testimony, suborning perjury. Either way, whether you apply the Toney standard, whether you apply the Maglov standard, both of them clearly qualify as proof beyond a reasonable doubt that contempt was committed, interference with witnesses was committed but I'm just raising that for the Court's attention. I used the term "suborning perjury." The definition of "to suborn" is "to secretly induce to do an unlawful thing." "To suborn is to secretly induce to do an unlawful thing." That comes from the Merriam-Webster dictionary. And perjury, of course, is lying under oath. So suborning perjury is "to secretly induce somebody to lie under oath." And that is this case. Beqa Beqaj induced secretly B1 to commit perjury. Now, what is the evidence of that? What is the conduct that supports that? The evidence in this case proved that Beqa Beqaj was perfectly situated to suborn B1's personally. He is was related by marriage to Isak Musliu; he was friends with B1 and his family and as such he was in the middle, he had contacts with both people, and he could carry out the job that was being asked. The evidence proved that Beqaj was seeking to convince B1 to lie or to withhold evidence to protect his in-laws, Musliu and Fatmir Limaj. Nothing more, nothing less. You have testimony from B1 that he received calls from his relative starting in early September, two months just prior to the start of the Limaj trial. He testified that these calls were simple and they contained two messages primarily: Call Beqaj, call Beqa Beqaj. Come to Kosovo to withdraw your statement. Not to testify truthfully, not to come tell everything you know about the horrible incident at the Lapusnik camp where people were massacred and brutalised. Come and withdraw your statement. The purpose of this was to get B1 to call Beqaj so that Beqaj could do his job which was to suborn perjury, as I said. Beqaj has incited the relative to participate in this contemptuous act. This is the evidence that pertains to incitement, as I said. Now, B1 testifies quite clearly the purpose of calling Beqaj. Beqaj is to convince B1 to make arrangements to go to Kosovo to secure the withdrawal of his testimony to recant -- in other words, to say you have nothing. That's the language that he uses, say you have nothing, or at the very least, send at least have B1 send a letter or a fax. Beqaj's role was to close this deal, to suborn personally, to arrange the withdrawal of this testimony. Not as to all three but as to two of the three. And that's a very key point for Your Honours to consider. Now, the key evidence of course is the two recorded calls between B1 on B1 and Beqa Beqaj which occur on October 6th and October 13th. Your Honours have the amazing luxury in this case of having the two principal criminal acts completely recorded. You don't need to assess the credibility of these witnesses. You don't need to judge the quality of their memory. You can listen to Beqa Beqaj's actual words without the filter of any witness. Now, the first call on October 6th. In this call, it is clear that there is no other subject matter in this call other than suborning perjury. They don't talk about the weather. They don't talk about other events in their life. After a few statements of pleasantries, the entire substance of that conversation, which is six or seven pages of transcript, is the simple message, I'm -- Beqa Beqaj is acting on behalf of Isak Musliu and you must say you have no evidence against Musliu and Limaj. Again, he's not saying tell the truth. Tell you what you know about the Lapusnik camp. He's saying say you have no evidence against Musliu and Limaj. Suborning perjury. Your Honour, I just want to confirm that you are getting the audio and the video clips that we are showing because the audience does not appear to be getting it. We have been showing some slides in this opening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I must say that I did not follow the intercepts or did not read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: They were just slides so far and you haven't missed the best evidence that we have so it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. But would you mind drawing my attention to that. If you're going to be showing slides, please, let me know.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Based on the incriminating evidence of the call, the first call on October 6th, the OTP determines that a criminal act has occurred. We file an application in Pristina, in Kosovo, to get a wire-tap, which is granted by the Court based on our evidence that we assert in our application, and a wire-tap of Beqa Beqaj's phone is conducted from October 13th through October 18th and Beqa Beqaj's calls are intercepted and recorded. And during this trial, you have heard these calls. There was a second call between B1 and Beqa Beqaj and, again, this call has no other subject matter than witness testimony, and I would like to draw your attention to the fact that Beqa Beqaj is related to Isak Musliu and he's talking to a witness in a trial against Isak Musliu. That in and of itself should send up alarm bells. But you also heard four other intercepted calls. These calls clearly demonstrate the extent of Beqaj's involvement and his conduct in this operation. These calls involve Demir Limaj, the brother of Fatmir Limaj; Salih Dull Bajrami who is a guard at the Lapusnik camp, and is also related to Beqa Beqaj and to Isak Musliu; and an unidentified man who talks with Beqaj about witnesses. They all use coded language. Some explicitly refer to witnesses and testimony. And now we have put up a slide just to refresh your memory as to one of these intercepted calls. Not only is this irrefutable evidence of Beqaj's connection to Musliu, but the coded language they use clearly demonstrates they are talking about criminal activity, suborning B1's perjurious testimony. And they know it's criminal. It also confirms Beqaj's own statement to B1 that he's acting on behalf of Isak Musliu in making these communications. Now finally, you have Beqaj's suspect interviews which take place on October 19 and October 21. And this interview contains his admission that he spoke to only one witness. They advised him that he had a right to a lawyer and he stopped and spontaneously uttered, "I don't need a lawyer because I've only spoken to one witness." And that's an admission that he has done exactly what we have accused him of doing. Now in these interviews, on October 19th in particular, he denies all involvement and he's lying. He says, I don't know anything about witnesses in the Limaj trial. I don't know any witnesses in the Limaj trial. And he's lying. These irrefutable lies show unmistakably one thing: his consciousness of guilt. Now, on October 21, another suspect interview takes place and again, he continues to lie, also showing his consciousness of guilt and that he's covering up for criminal behaviour. But in this interview he's confronted directly with the evidence of the intercepts that catch him red-handed and he ultimately, although not completely he ultimately relents and says, yes, I have spoken to Witness B1 but B1 called me, I didn't call B1. That was his excuse. And he also says, Well, yes, I did speak to Isak Musliu and in that conversation, it's very clear that he admits that he's talking about witnesses with Isak Musliu. But he's saying look it's not me, these people are calling me. So right now I want to play some of the -- just a few clips, Your Honour, from the recorded calls and the purpose is to highlight the language that Beqa Beqaj uses in these clips. And you will note -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We then should move into private session if we play these clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think I can go in public session until -- and I can alert you when we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I wanted to point out that as you listen to these, you will notice that you will never hear Beqa Beqaj say to this witness, who is a vulnerable witness, who is in deep witness protection, has been -- there were two assassination attempts on his life, he never testifies to that witness -- testified truthfully, say what you know about this horrible event. What he says is, say you have no evidence. Can you put up the first clip?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Say you have nothing to do with Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu. Play the next clip. If AV could stop the audio to the public on this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm being informed that we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go into private session, please, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: In these recorded conversations he used the language "fix up" which has no other connotation other than suborning perjury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Okay. For this first one. Briefly we'll need to go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's move into private session, please. Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please proceed, Mr. Akerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: In these recorded calls he also uses language, such as "give us some help." "Do a good deed." "Do a good deed for all of the Albanian people," referring to these people, Isak Musliu and Fatmir Limaj, who by some people are seen as heroes in that country and if he withdraws the testimony that is incriminating against them, that he's doing a good deed for the Albanian people. And I want to show one last clip because he also uses this language.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: "About Bala, I won't press you there. Nothing." "About Bala, I won't press you there." The inference you can draw from that is that as to the others he is going to press them because he is clearly pressing as to the other two but as to Bala he's applying no pressure. So they are being very selective about what evidence they want to suborn perjury on. Now, there was some indication by a witness that Beqa Beqaj is a mere messenger, he's a go-between between Isak Musliu and B1 and the evidence does not support that he is just a simply a messenger. He's fully engaged in conduct to influence B1's testimony. This is a public session clip so I can show this clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: What Beqa Beqaj says in this clip is, "Come to Kosovo at my expense." He's been authorised, and he's a poor villager, you heard testimony that he's not a wealthy man, but he's been authorised to pay for the expenses of this witness. That's how important this job is that Beqa Beqaj has been handed, that he's empowered to pay for the expenses of somebody to travel from this foreign country back to Kosovo to make a statement to say he's got nothing on Limaj and Musliu. He is not only authorised as to expenses, he's authorised to guarantee -- and he makes guarantees of safety and that can only happen in conjunction with being aligned with powerful people in Kosovo. I'm going to show you one clip as to guarantees of safety. This one, Your Honour, needs to be closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Further evidence of the fact that Beqa Beqaj is not a mere messenger is the fact that he is authorised to make arrangements as to whether or not B1 returns to Kosovo or simply sends a fax or a letter, and that's repeated several times in the record. And he's also -- he makes several arrangements as to -- or he makes several offers as to the arrangements that B1, where he could go to meet. It could be at one person's house, it could be at another person's house. But Beqa Beqaj can guarantee safety; he can indicate to the witness that he can testify by letter or by fax; he can arrange a meeting place; he can pay expenses. He is not a mere messenger in this. He is involved in the suborning of perjury. Now another aspect of the intercepted telephone calls is the coded language, as I said. And the coded language demonstrates that all parties had knowledge that what they were doing was criminal. But you can also infer that much more is going on. I'm going to play a few clips here but some of the inferences, some of the statements are -- and in fact, one of the participants says, "can you talk on the phone?" And the answer is, "No. I can't talk on the phone." And these are all conversations about witnesses -- and about B1, frankly, because they all take place within two hours, two, three hours after B1 and Beqaj's call. And it's very clear that everyone knows the code, because when Isak Musliu, for instance, calls Beqa Beqaj and they talk, he says, "Has the roof been put on the house?" And B1 himself said, I know that Isak Musliu is not in the construction business from prison. They are talking about a job being unfinished and that job being unfinished is Beqa Beqaj's perjurious testimony has not been secured. But Beqa Beqaj doesn't say "I don't know what you're talking about. What are you talking about with a house with no roof?" He says "I got you." He knows exactly what's going on. He's fully involved. I am going to play a few clips and these are all public session clips.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: There is a couple of interesting aspects about this intercepted phone call. One, they refer to the 5.00 call and I would reminds the Court that the 5.00 call is the call between B1 and Beqa Beqaj. These are subsequent conversations where they are talking about the 5.00 call. Beqa acknowledges that it's him on the phone. He says that B1 was angry and he says "The business looks better now," "The business looks better now." So they are speculating on whether or not B1 is likely to come through, because, as you recall, on the October 13th call, the way it was ended is that B1 says, "I'm not saying anything now. I may, I may not. I don't know." What's related from that conversation is it's looking better now. And what that means is that Beqa Beqaj is not only talking to B1 but he's talking to other people about this. He's involved in it. He's involved in the suborning of perjury. Can you play the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Now, this is the coded language that I just referred to. This is Isak Musliu and Beqa Beqaj. "The beams weren't done. The roof wasn't put up." "He went back on his word, the head of the house," and you can tell that there is -- it's coded language but it has two different subject matters one is talking about a person who has gone back on his word. That is B1, who has gone back on his word that he is not going to suborn perjury. "The head of the house has gone back on his word. Now the roof can't be put up." What's interesting is that Beqa Beqaj doesn't say "I don't know what you are talking here. What are you talking about with this roof?" Let's go to the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: In this clip, an intercepted call: "We have got to meet by all means in order to get it right." "Can't you speak over the phone?" "I can't." "So can we meet in this place?" "Yes, let's meet in this place." They know that it's dangerous to talk on the phone; they are engaged in a criminal -- in criminal conduct, suborning perjury; they are not going to do it over the phone. They all know what's going on, and they decide to meet. Let's go to the next clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Again, you have a reference - this is Isak Musliu, now - to the owner of the house and he says here, in frankly one of the more chilling passages, "What's with him? He should have been told straight." And recall that according to B1, Isak Musliu had tried to assassinate him and Isak Musliu says, "Neither the moon nor the heaven, nothing can rescue him from that business. Just so things are known. Speak to him once more. Tell him so, and tell him quite bluntly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, may I interrupt you, Mr. Akerson? Who is B2?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: In this particular case, the phone has been handed over to Bashkim Beqaj. In that conversation with Isak Musliu the phone initially was picked up by Beqa Beqaj and that was identified by B1 as Beqa Beqaj and in the middle of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just want things to be clear. B2 is not Mr. Beqaj?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: All of these coded conversations, Your Honour, reflect the scope of this operation and corroborate that the sole purpose of this activity was criminal, it was to suborn the perjury of B1, to interfere with B1's truthful testimony. And everyone knew it. Now, I have mentioned that B1 was lying and had lied in his suspect interview and that indicates consciousness of guilt. And I just want to spend a quick moment looking at these lies a little more carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting. You said that B1 was -- B1 was lying and had lied.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Sorry, that's my mistake. Beqaj is lying in these interviews. Beqa Beqaj is interviewed on October 19th and October 21st and he's lying throughout and that is indication of his consciousness of guilt. The first lie that Beqa Beqaj tells is that he can't speak -- he can't recall speaking to B1. And of course you yourselves heard two recorded conversations on October 6th and October 13th where they were speaking. Irrefutable evidence he's lying. Beqa Beqaj claims he didn't know B1 was a witness and again you heard two recorded calls. You don't need to rely on any witness's memory, October 6, October 13th, where he's speaking to B1 about his testimony. Irrefutably, it's a lie. Beqa Beqaj claims that he didn't have a telephone call with Dull, Salih Bajrami. I do want to play -- if you can play the second -- this is public testimony as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Tells in the interview that he didn't have a call with Salih Dull Bajrami, the first thing in this intercepted call is "Where are you Beqa?" "I'm at home." "It's Dull on the phone." It's Salih Bajrami. He's lying. And he's lying because of a consciousness of guilt. Beqa claims that he had not spoken or spoken with or knew Demir Limaj. Now in all of his conversations with B1, he says, "You're going to meet with Demir Limaj." I want to play you a clip on that one. You can play the second one which is open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: And here, Beqa Beqaj in his own words says, "I have talked to Fatmir Limaj's brother, that Demir, and a they send their greetings in this matter." It's a lie. He lied to the investigators. Now, if all he was doing was trying to secure the truthful testimony of a witness, he would not need to lie about it. He's lying because he knows what he's doing. He's suborning perjury. One other aspect of the evidence that I'd like to comment on which is the sequence of the calls, because I think it's very important for you to fully understand. On October 13th, there are four calls are made. At 2.00, there is a call between Isak Musliu and Beqa Beqaj on October 13th. At 5.00 there is a call between Witness B1 and Beqa Beqaj. And immediately thereafter, an hour and a half later, there is a call between somebody we don't know and Beqa Beqaj talking about the 5.00 call. An hour after that there is a call between Salih Dull Bajrami and Beqa Beqaj, also speaking in coded language about witnesses. And then the next day, there is a call between Demir Limaj and Bashkim Beqaj on the phone. And they are all talking about witness testimony. And it just corroborates, again, the extent of involvement and how concerned these people were with securing this perjurious testimony of B1. I've talked a little bit about the incitement evidence so I'm not going to play you any clips. I'm just going to through what the incitement evidence is. Beqa employs a relative to get B1 to call. He incites this relative to participate in the interference with a witness. B1 testifies that this is a pattern, that his family has been continually subjected to these kind of encounters where people approach his family and ask them to contact him to persuade him not to testify. B1 testifies that this relative tells him that he must go to Kosovo to meet with Beqaj to withdraw his statement. So this relative isn't saying, "Just call Beqaj," he's also saying - and he's been put up to this by Beqa Beqaj - that "you need to not only call Beqa Beqaj but you need to arrange to go there so that you can withdraw your testimony." And the October 6th call, the first recorded call that we have between Beqa Beqaj and B1 confirms this because the first thing -- B1 calls Beqa Beqaj and one of the first things he says is, "My relative says I'm supposed to call you." Which confirms everything B1 said about that. That's incitement. He was inciting this relative to participate in this scheme. In short, you have two recorded calls between Beqa Beqaj and B1 and you have the intercepted calls on Beqaj's phone. All of these pertain to witness testimony. All of which lead to one inexorable conclusion: That Beqaj's conduct and his intent was to secure B1's perjurious testimony, nothing more, nothing less. B1 was engaging in conduct intended to and to influence B1's evidence. I just have a couple of other point that I want to talk about, other evidence. There was -- there is evidence that B1's calls Beqaj and I know Defence counsel asked a question about that so I wanted to address that. B1 on October 6 in fact calls Beqa Beqaj. What is the relevance of that? B1 calls Beqaj, not the other way around. Absolutely none. Has no relevance to this case. First of all, B1 was supposed to call Beqaj because the relative was badgering him to call and he was finally relenting. And in fact he relented at the urging of the Office of the Prosecutor who said let's record it so we find out what's going on. So that is not only expected, it's exactly what we had asked him to do. Secondly, it doesn't matter. Who calls who doesn't matter. If B1 had called Beqaj, if Beqaj had called B1, if they are on the phone and Beqaj threatens him, intimidates him or in this case interferes with his truthful testimony in any way, it's a crime. It doesn't matter who called who. It's irrelevant. Now there is evidence that B1 and B2 don't feel threatened by Beqaj and they both made very nice statements about what a nice guy Beqaj is and that may very well be true. But what is the relevance of that? What is the relevance of whether or not he's a nice guy? Absolutely none. It has no relevance to this case whatsoever. In fact, it strengthens our case, because our whole theory is that Isak Musliu could not have contacted B1 himself. B1 would have never taken the call from somebody who had attempted to assassinate him. He had to find people that would be persuasive and so he is going to find people that are in the inner circle of B1. So the fact that he's a friend and that he's been identified by Isak Musliu completely supports the theory and fits in with every piece of evidence that you have in this case that they needed to find family and friends to contact these witnesses in order to suborn perjury. And I would also like to point out that under the Maglov definition of interference where it says "likely to deter," it's far more likely that Beqa Beqaj would be able to deter a witness that he knows that he's friends with than Isak Musliu would be. So it strengthens, it does nothing but strengthen our case. I want to just touch on the notion of threat. It's not a threat case. We had never proceeded on it. But the simple fact is that the ominous language that Isak Musliu uses in that intercepted phone call is threatening. The fact that Isak Musliu's name is used in these communications to a witness who he knew - he attempted to assassinate, that he had put in a prison camp and brutalised, he knew that one of his relatives had been killed in that camp - the mere mention of Isak Musliu is a threatening presence and it's an implied threat. It's not necessary because you have clear, ample evidence of witness interference without going to the area of threat, but Isak Musliu's name is invoked continuously and that is an implied threat. There is no evidence in this case or wasn't clear what Beqa Beqaj's motive was in this. He may have been motivated by some financial gain; he may have been motivated because he doesn't like B1; He may have been motivated by the influence of his relatives. It doesn't really matter. What is the relevance of motive? It doesn't matter. If a burglar breaks into a house, whether he's doing it because he hates the people who live there, he hates the homeowners or whether he's doing it because of financial gain, it's irrelevant, he's committed a crime. Whatever Beqa Beqaj's motives are for suborning perjury in this case are irrelevant. He committed a crime. Doesn't matter why. Now, last but not least, B1 in his conversations with Beqaj sometimes downplays the evidence that he has on Isak Musliu and Fatmir Limaj and he says things like, look, Beqa, I don't have that much on Limaj. I don't have that much on Musliu. And what is the significance of that? It could be argued that all that Beqa Beqaj was asking him to do was to come and tell -- make a truthful statement. So what is the significance of that? Absolutely nothing. There is no significance. Interference is interference, and whether Beqa Beqaj was interfering with a very valuable witness in the Limaj case or whether he was interfering with a completely irrelevant witness in the Limaj case, it doesn't matter. He's making efforts to suborn perjury. It doesn't matter. But factually, you need to be aware that you have his ebb tire -- you have B1's entire testimony from the Limaj trial and it's very clear that there was lots of evidence that B1 had on Fatmir Limaj and Isak Musliu, and common sense would just dictate that they would not have gone to all this effort to secure this perjurious testimony if there wasn't something there they were worried about. And it's perfectly natural for B1 who is vulnerable - he's been in witness protection, he's had assassination attempts and threats on his life - he's speaking to someone he knows as a relative of the accused in the Limaj trial, and he's not going to be forthcoming and say, here is all of the incriminating evidence I have on your uncle. He's going to say, look I don't have that much because the more he says, the more evidence he says he has on the Limaj accused, the more danger he's in. And he knows that there is a direct communication between Beqa Beqaj and Isak Musliu. So the fact that in these conversations he says I don't have that much on Limaj or Musliu is irrelevant. But there are a couple of key passages here and I want to just play one because this is very important. And I think this one has to be closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The evidence in this case, Your Honour, is clear and unequivocal. Beqa Beqaj acted to suborn perjury of a key witness in the Limaj trial, a witness that was vulnerable, a witness that was protected. You have the inherent power under Rule 77 to enter findings of contempt. You also have the duty to protect the witnesses in this case. You have the duty to protect the integrity of these proceedings. You have the duty to protect the integrity of these trials. Witnesses must be inviolate if they are going to have the ability to come to this Tribunal and not fear for their lives and not feel like they are be badgered or interfered with or threatened or intimidated. We are asking to you use your inherent power in this case to send a strong and clear message that we won't tolerate it this kind of interference with witnesses. We are asking to you find Beqa Beqaj guilty of contempt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Akerson. May I ask you one question for clarification. Right at the end of your closing argument, you used a word in the singular, interfered with a witness. Do you mean one witness or two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Beqa Beqaj only interfered with one witness. The assertions in the indictment was that a relative of Beqa Beqaj and indirectly Beqa Beqaj -- a relative of Beqa Beqaj had confronted B2 directly and, indirectly, Beqa Beqaj had confronted that witness. But as it turns out at trial that evidence was not developed, and so we are sticking with the strong part of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make sure: You maintain your position against the accused on the basis or as far as B1 is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we started off, I asked you this question, and you said that two witnesses had been interfered with, B1 and B2, and -- the witness and the potential witness, and now you are adopting a different position, if I've understood you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I think I'll -- I'll maintain my original position that under the standards that -- under the Toney case, both witnesses were interfered with. B2, obviously, is a lesser interference. The main case is against B1 and that is the strength of our argument. But I'll stand by the original statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you stand by both witnesses, in other words a witness and the potential witness, B1 and B2?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. van der Spoel, I'm now turning to the Defence team. We have 20 minutes. Would you like to make a break now or would you like to present your closing arguments and we have the break after that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: I would like to have the break now, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We shall now have a 30-minute break, and resume at 5 minutes to 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van der Spoel, I will now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Prosecutor, Registry. My closing arguments I would like to present also in written form, Your Honour. I have copies for the Bench, for the Prosecutor, and of course also for the Registrar. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I've understood you correctly, this is a summary of your closing argument; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Very correct, Your Honour. It's a summary and most of my closing arguments. Sometimes I will leave the written closing arguments and go into oral argument. But it's a summary of my closing argument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will start with an introduction and then analyse the incidents as presented by the Prosecutor. Then I will go into the statements of my client as made during this trial. I of course will discuss some law issues as requested, and I will finish my summing up with some remarks on punishment. Your Honours, the introduction. The Prosecution has not made it easy for the Defence to determine what the exact accusations are against my client. The indictment is vague and I have argued in the pre-Defence brief the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief lacks the specificities my client is entitled to regarding the evidence on each charge as formulated in Rule 65. During the Pre-Trial Conference on the 25th of April last week, the Prosecutor answered to a question from the Bench that the charges pertain to both B1 and B2. The counts are still, according to the Prosecutor during his opening statement, contempt; attempted contempt; incitement to contempt. In his opening statement, the Prosecutor gives some clarity. This case is primarily a case of witness interference and bribery as opposed to threats or intimidations. Witnesses B1 and B2 are the targets. But even today, Mr. President, the Prosecutor seems to have difficulty to formulate the exact criminal offence Beqa Beqaj is accused of. Let's look at the incidents. The Prosecutor maintains that there are six incidents that apparently justify the hazy accusations. In first instance, these incidents will have to be proven to have taken place. Then Beqa Beqaj's involvement as meant in Rule 77 will have to be proven beyond a reasonable doubt. I will now analyse these incidents to see if any relevant evidence has been presented by the Prosecution on trial. The Defence wishes at this point to underline that it persists in the views, as formulated in the Defence pre-trial brief. Incident 1, Your Honours. The encounter between Witness B2 and my client's son, the only incident in which B2 is involved. B2's testimony on trial gives evidence that Bashkim acted aggressively and blamed B2 for his uncle's imprisonment in The Hague. It also shows that Beqa Beqaj has nothing to do with his son's behaviour and he felt badly about it. I quote the witness, "And I said to him, your son nearly beat me in Shtime," in reference to this matter. "They felt very bad about it. Though invited me in inside, offer me coffee and tea and they felt very bad about it. They wondered how come their son did that to me. He said to me that Isak Musliu had called him six times from The Hague and told him to come to me, and I didn't want to do that." Another quote: "At that point in the summer of last year, do you know, did Beqa Beqaj know that you and B1 were potential witnesses in The Hague?" Answer: "No, I don't think he knew about it." Another quotation: "You are in the middle of answering. Can you please -- I think you are -- I believe you are saying that Beqaj was telling you that Isak Musliu wanted you and Murat wanted to do something. Can you please continue from that point?" Answer from the witness: "Beqaj said to me that is what he said, and I intended to tell you this. And since you were in conflict with my son, that is why I'm telling you this." This -- the rest of the quotation is quite important, Your Honour, "But he didn't have the intention to tell me to help them in any concrete way." As Your Honours will remember, B2 had a last request. He underlined that Beqa Beqaj is a good person and would really wish him to be set free and for them to go back home together, not because my client is a good guy, because my client did not commit a criminal offence at all. Incidents 2, 3 and 4, Your Honours. As already stipulated in the Defence pre-trial brief, the incidents 2, 3 and 4 describe alleged contacts that Beqa Beqaj would have held through a relative whose name we now know. This relative was initially on the Prosecutor's witness list but for unknown reasons, he was withdrawn. I think that's a very important circumstance in this case. During the summing up of the Prosecutor, he made assumptions about what happened with that witness, the communication between that relative and my client. But it remains unclear, only assumptions. The most important person who could elaborate on that was the relative, and why wasn't the relative heard by the Prosecutor? Why didn't the relative present evidence at the trial? It's something to ponder about, Your Honour. Something to think about. Regarding the background information connected to assassination attempts B1 gave during his testimony, I would like to quote the following. "Is Mr. Beqaj connected in any way with these incidents?" Prosecutor answered: "Not that we are aware of, no." My client has nothing to do with the background information as presented on trial by Inspector Sutch. He has nothing to do with the trial. He has nothing to do with those suspects. No evidence has been delivered. B1 is quite clear who took the initiative to make contact. Beqaj never called him. If he wanted to, he could have done. That's what the witness said under oath on trial. The Prosecutor made the assumption that there was quite a deal of collaboration between the relative and my client to communicate with B1. Your Honours, if that were the case, wouldn't it be so that the relative would have given the telephone number to my client? Because B1 did communicate with the relative. The relative could phone with B1. So if there would have been a collaboration, then it would have been very simple for the relative to give that telephone number to my client, and my client would have, in the view of the Prosecution, phoned with the Witness B1. So I think it's a very important factor in this case who called and why didn't my client call. The relative phoned B1 frequently with a request that B1 should phone with Beqa Beqaj. During the contacts between the relative, B1, and B1's mother, land was mentioned but not in relation to the withdrawal of B1's testimony. That's what B1 testified on trial. The incidents 5 and 6. We all know the contents of the intercepted telephone calls between B1 and my client. I would like to remark that the translations of these conversations are not always, how shall I say, satisfactory. During the testimony of B1, the Bench correctly pointed out that the English word "business" was not the only meaning of the Albanian word that was used during the conversation. I've also discovered that the two telephone interceptions on the 13th of October last year were not in part correct and complete. The latest translations, however, are more satisfactory. I just want to say, as a general remark, it is very, very dangerous to rely on the interpretations in a telephone calls especially if they are being translated from a language that we ourselves do not use. Some specific remarks regarding incident 5, Your Honours. This apparently relates to a telephone conversation that my client had with Witness B1. The transcript does not in any way give the impression of a man, my client, pressuring another man, B1. The telephone conversation is initiated by Witness B1. The Prosecutor's allegation that B1 is to declare that he has nothing to do with it disregards the context and the nature of the conversation. (redacted) (redacted). This forms the evidence that Mr. Beqaj only wants B1 to declare what he is saying himself, not to commit perjury, what the Prosecution today is trying to say. Beqaj does not in any way pressure, coerce or influence B1. He is just asking B1 to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. van der Spoel, I'm sorry to interrupt but does Mr. Beqaj have any problem? I've noticed that he may not be able to follow the proceedings. Mr. Beqaj, can you hear us properly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I can hear you correctly, and I am happy with what is being said here by my Defence attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to make sure that you could hear properly, that you could hear everything that is being said in this courtroom. I'm sorry, Mr. van der Spoel, for having interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Thank, Your Honour. I would now like to make some specific remarks regarding the last incident, incident 6. This alleges that coded language is being used, for which assertion there is no proof at all. It is an unfounded conclusion. The context of this conversation, whatever is being said, cannot bring clarity as to the nature of it. Again, even if the conversation would be about B1 or anybody else testifying before the Tribunal, the conversation as recorded is too vague to indicate or to interpret this in an incriminating manner towards the accused. As far as this example discusses the things that were said in the second telephone conversations of that day, the Defence argues that even if my client would have said these things, the accused doesn't ask anything else than to declare what the witness is saying himself: The truth. I would like to react to the summing up of the Prosecutor he just made. He also talked about a lot of other telephone conversations. I would like to stipulate that there is no evidence at all that my client was aware of those telephone conversations. There are only two telephone conversations between B1 and my client, and the rest of the telephone conversations, for example, between his son and one of the suspects or accused in The Hague, there is no evidence for at all. Your Honours, B1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: B1 gives some clarity during his testimony on trial. B1 is not afraid of my client. He is not someone who threatens him but someone who supports him in his fortune. (redacted) (redacted) B1 testifies quote, "As for the first call that I made to Beqaj, I informed the investigator that my intention was to find out whether Beqaj knows the level of threat. All I wanted was to find out what was being said about me and what was the level of threat. I never thought that Beqaj would be here arrested. I just wanted to know in order to be able to defend myself so that I could make measures to stay in my apartment and not leave it. As I said, I never thought that it this would lead to Beqaj's arrest." To the questions from the Bench, the witness said the following: "Honourable Judges, if we look at the entire statement or the phone registered telephone calls, according to everything it turned out that he is closer to me than my brothers. Nobody can tell what he has in his heart. When he tells me that I can stand by your side in case you need to take revenge for your father, then this is no threat for me. I have declared to the Prosecutors and I declare here to this Tribunal, that Beqa Beqaj has never intimidated what -- threatened me and was never expect him to do that." B1 also says in this part of the testimony quite clearly that the word "threat" was never mentioned. B1 also denies that he would be given land in exchange for his withdrawing his testimony. The evidence delivered by the third Prosecution witness, Sutch, is only relevant to confirm that Beqa Beqaj has indeed been interviewed and that these interviews have been registered in the correct way; no more, no less. Such views and interpretations of the content of the telephone interceptions are irrelevant and can in no way be used as evidence in this case. As Sutch testifies, it is difficult for him to comment on these telephone calls. It is really the perception of the individual that hears the words. So no evidence at all for the Prosecution. The Prosecutor just made a remark about Beqa Beqaj's statements. I would like to say the following about the statements my client made. Regarding these interviews, and his reluctancy in the beginning to answer all the questions, this cannot be used against him. As mentioned in the Defence pre-trial brief, Beqa Beqaj later on agreed to be interviewed by the Prosecutor. He also made a statement on trial as provided in Article 84 of the rules. In this context, Your Honours, I would like to point out paragraph 47 of the Nobilo judgement: "Although there were many inconsistencies within the various statements made by Mr. Nobilo concerning other issues which could have discredited him as a witness in relation to these issues, a mere disbelief of a witness's denial of a particular fact does not by itself logically permit a Tribunal affect to accept beyond reasonable doubt the truth of fact which he denied." It's a decision of the 30th of May 2001. Your Honours, I would like to leave the facts and go to some issues of law. Some issues of law will now be discussed to determine that Beqa Beqaj's behaviour cannot be qualified as a criminal offence as meant in Rule 77. Whatever the Prosecutor may have meant in his indictment and pre-trial brief, it is clear that Beqa Beqaj did not threaten a witness, meaning "an expression of an intention to inflict pain, injury, evil or punishment." He did not intimidate a witness, meaning "to make timid, to fill with fear." He did not bribe a witness, meaning "something such as money or a favour offered or given to a person in a position of privilege or trust to influence that person's view or conduct in the other person's favour." These not proven elements of Rule 77 are examples of the general notion of interference as meant in Rule 77. It is our submission that interference as such has no specific meaning. In the Defence pre-trial brief we made a passing reference to jurisdiction and the principles of nullum crimen sine lege. We argue that the blanket term, interference, violates this principle of legality. In this regard, I would like to quote Goran Sluiter in his article "The ICTY and Offences Against the Administration of Justice," Journal of International Criminal Justice 2004, page 631 and further. He says the following: "When examining the various contempt cases of the Tribunal, a number of issues are problematic. One of these has already been examined above and concerns the jurisdictional basis of the contempt law. A consequence of the adopted common-law approach is the lack of a firmly-established set of offences. As a result, confusion may ensue as to the elements of various forms of contempt, for example, concerning the Prosecution -- the Prosecution of alleged contempt by counsel Nobilo, the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Trial Chamber reached different conclusions as to the required mens rea." It is our submission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Sorry, Mr. van der Spoel, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour. It is our submission, Your Honours, that interference must have something to do with the obstruction of justice. See, for example, Article 70 of the Rome Statute of the Criminal Court, paragraph 1 under C: "and must be translated to actions of the accused that amounts to specific behaviour comparable to threats and the other elements as mentioned in Rule 77." Beqa Beqaj did not commit any of these contempt elements but also did not attempt or instigate this crime. Attempt is, according to Cassese -- I quote him in his book, International Criminal Law, Oxford, 2003, page 1895 and further -- "clearly what is required for the attempt to be punishable is, firstly, conduct consisting of a significant commencement of the criminal action." He gives an example that's not relevant for this case. "The second element is the clear intention to commit a crime and failure of that intention to take effect owing to external circumstances." Again the question arises, who did Beqa Beqaj attempt to interfere with? There is also no evidence of contact -- of conduct consisting of significant commencement of an action as required in Rule 77. Instigation of the crime of contempt is unthinkable when you look at the facts. Who did my client intentionally prompt or provoke to commit contact? The relative? Where is the proof of that? There is no proof at all. Rule 77, Your Honours, also prescribes that the acts must be committed knowingly and wilfully. ICTY case law shows that it must be established that the accused acted with specific intent to interfere with the Tribunal's administration of justice. See, for example, the Nobilo contempt case. In summary, Your Honours, Beqa Beqaj has not fulfilled above-mentioned criteria to commit the crime of contempt as prescribed in Rule 77. The contacts Beqa Beqaj had with B1 and B2 did not interfere with the administration of justice. In this regard, the Defence still submits that the Prosecutor also has not delivered sufficient evidence that Beqa Beqaj had knowledge of the fact that B1 and B2 were witnesses or potential witnesses in ICTY trials, nor that he had knowledge of the existence of Rule 77 as we have submitted in our pre-trial Defence brief. Proof beyond a reasonable doubt must be established in order to support a finding of contempt. This proof can only be established through substantial and credible evidence. This standard and burden of proof has not been met by the Prosecutor, and therefore, it is our submission that Beqa Beqaj must be acquitted. Your Honours, I understand that the Prosecutor does not want any punishment because the Prosecutor has not answered your request about Article -- sorry, Rule 86 and paragraph 3 so I would like to know from the Bench if you want me to make some remarks about punishment, even though of course I do submit that the client should be acquitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that I will first ask the Prosecution to tell us about this matter, because they have the right to reply to you, and then you will have the right to respond to what they will reply yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Akerson, I believe that you are the one who is going to speak now. You will respond to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure you've heard the comments of Mr. van der Spoel, and I believe that the Chamber has invited you to fulfil the conditions provided for by Rule 86(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, where it is stated that during the closing arguments, the parties shall also address matters of sentencing.

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do intend on addressing the matter of sentencing in this rebuttal, this very brief rebuttal. First I'm just going to respond very briefly to a couple of matters that the Defence raised. First of all, Defence raises the matter of Witness B2 testifying. And what I would respond is that you have witnesses who are human beings. In this case B2 was or is a 69-year-old witness who is testifying for him in completely unfamiliar surroundings, under very traumatic circumstances. Human beings have memories which are fallible. Mine, my colleagues', everyone in this room. Recordings of intercepted phone calls are infallible. What's on that recording does not change. It is not filtered through anyone's memory. The best evidence you have of the criminal act in this case is the recordings, which is not to disparage the witnesses. They may have done their best but witnesses are human beings. So whatever lapses may have occurred, you have two incidences that are recorded that are the best evidence in this case. The Defence raises the point that there are no calls from Beqaj to B1. It's irrelevant. It does not matter. It absolutely misses the point. And it contradicts the evidence. October 6 recorded call, indisputable evidence. The first -- one of the first things that is said

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: The Defence says there is no evidence as to what the relative was -- what he did, and that simply is not the case. B1 testified a number of occasions that this relative contacted him and said that he is to call Beqaj in order to withdraw his statement, make arrangements. Now, that's evidence. You give it whatever weight you want but it's evidence and the Defence cannot say that there isn't evidence. The Defence claims that there was no evidence of pressure and there is a recorded call, October 6, where the language, "we are not pressing you as to Bala," it's clear pressure. It's a clear statement of pressure. You don't have to rely on a witness. You don't have to try to interpret what somebody said. You have it right there. The issue of the quality of translations is an issue for pre-trial. The two translations that were raised as problematic by the Defence were retranslated by us without contest and we submitted them as they were retranslated. If the Defence had had any issue with any of our translations that's a matter for pre-trial and we could have addressed it. It cannot be raised at trial at this stage. The Defence raises the issue of the coded language and says they are too vague to make sense out of. In the context of those calls, the four calls put together, they make perfect sense. They are indisputably about witness testimony and the bottom line is, Your Honours, criminals speak in code when they are protecting their criminal conduct. They are not going to say, I'm talking here about suborning witness testimony, suborning perjury. They talk in code so that they aren't caught. That's what they do. Of course it's going to be vague but we as human beings and as experienced investigators have the ability and -- the ability to interpret and infer the meaning. Defence says that Jonathan Sutch's testimony isn't evidence. Of course it is evidence. He's testifying as experienced investigator, based on his experience in that case as to his analysis of these calls, and that is clearly evidence. Defence raises the point that the intercepted calls don't pertain to Beqa Beqaj and I want to go through those one by one on that. Exhibit 2, which is an intercepted call. The first person says "hello," the second person says "where are you Beqa?" He says, "here at Shtime." And the other person says, "it's Dull speaking. Where are you?" The tape self-identifies, but it was also identified by B1 when he testified. Exhibit 3 line 12 in the transcript self-identifies, it says Beqa is on the phone. He's saying "I'm on the phone." He identifies himself. Exhibit 7, identified on the record by B1 as the voice of Beqa Beqaj. And the inference is easy to draw because the phone is picked up by a male who is familiar with what's going on, it's handed over to Bashkim Beqaj, his son, but it's clearly identified by B1 as Beqa Beqaj. So the assertion that these don't pertain to -- don't involve Beqa Beqaj is simply incorrect. Defence asserts in its argument that the element of a threat is required in interference, and that is not suggested by Rule 77, which distinguishes between threats, intimidations and interferences -- other interferences. If they were meant to be the same, it would have been constructed differently but the plain language in the rule distinguishes between those offences. Lastly, the Defence raises the issue that his client didn't know Rule 77. And I think it's a clear principle that ignorance of the law is not a defence. Very few of the accused that sit in any trial here probably would be aware of the statutes at the time they committed their offence. In some cases, -- well, I'll leave it at that. Very few of the accused have a complete or even a vague understanding of international humanitarian law. That is not a defence. Ignorance of the law is not a defence. As to sentence, Your Honour, I would cite only one aggravating factor, and that is that the victim in this case was a victim who is the most vulnerable of any of the victims that we have; had been in witness protection for months, if not years; had moved residence three times - three times - to secure his safety in the prior -- in the months leading up to trial. And still Beqa Beqaj is attempting to contact that witness through relatives at the behest of Isak Musliu in order to suborn perjury. This is a witness who survives a massacre; who survives the Lapusnik camp; survives two assassination attempts, one at the hands, allegedly, of Isak Musliu; his family is put through the excruciating pain of witness protection, not only through this institution but through two countries. And still, they were trying to get to this witness because of his importance. Our witnesses must remain inviolate and protected, especially the vulnerable witnesses amongst us. And that is an aggravating circumstance. That being said, the Prosecution also understands the mitigating circumstances in this case. We are only asking as a sentence for six months to be imposed by this Court. And I think that's all I have in rebuttal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Akerson. I'd like to ask you one question, a point of clarification. If we look at the documents in evidence in this case, we can see that on October 19th Mr. Beqaj was arrested. On October 19. Can you confirm that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I'll have to double check that. The date of arrest, I think that's accurate, Your Honour, but I will have to double check it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I'd like to direct your attention to the fact that the 19th of October was the day when we had the first interview with Mr. Beqaj. And during that interview, the only thing that was mentioned, the only matter that was mentioned was B2. No mention was made of B1. However, it was decided to proceed with the arrest. And if we look at the documents that we have, Mr. Beqaj was kept in detention, then the indictment was issued by the Prosecutor on the 21st. It was confirmed on the 28th. The initial appearance took place on the 8th of November. Therefore, the Chamber would like to know what was the status of Mr. Beqaj during the period starting with the October 19th. Are you in a position to answer my question now?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: I think that is correct, Your Honour, that he was -- he has -- he was in custody as of October 19th, until he was provisionally released in April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We know all the details. Thank you. Mr. van der Spoel, would you like to say anything in rejoinder?

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: Some very short remarks. Of course memories can cause failure in evidence, but the memory of B2, it wasn't something that happened long ago and he was quite detailed in his memory about the restaurant and about the food and about the drinks and things like that. And I think the Prosecutor's mistaken because involving B2 isn't any telephone interception. The interception is important for B1. So B2 could have course not talk about the telephone interception. He could only say well, I saw Bashkim, I went to his father, his father said oh, very sorry about that what's happening to my son? Well, I was phoned by Musliu but I don't want anything to do with it. That's what the witness said. The telephone calls weren't important for that part of the indictment, as I understand it. Back to the telephone calls. Of course the Prosecutor is right. When my client participates in a telephone conversation, he know about the telephone conversation, but the Prosecutor also mentioned some other telephone conversations in which my client did not participate and he did not have the knowledge of that telephone conversation. That's what I was trying to say. About the translations, I just made a remark that the first translation wasn't very satisfactory; the second was. And the other remark I made was instigated by the Bench. The Bench noticed the word "business" and asked the interpreters, is that what the Albanian word is? And then the interpret says something else and you can't blame me for not bringing it up in pre-trial. The judges did that on trial. I would like to make a remarks about -- perhaps I have not been clear about interference. If you read Article -- sorry, Rule 77, you read "some acts," "some elements," "threat," "bribe," and you have the blanket term "interference." If you talk about a criminal offence, you just can't call it interference. It has to be something else. It has to be something like a threat, like a bribe. That was what I was trying to say. And about the ignorance of the law. Of course the Prosecutor is right when you talk about the statute, about humanitarian law, and about war crimes and about genocide. That's in the statute. Article 77 is in the Rules, and the rules can be ambiguous, when a criminal offence is defined in the Rules, and if that rule is ambiguous, and you are not an officer of the court, and you are not an accused in the criminal proceedings, isn't it logical that the Prosecutor should prove that? I come to some other points I would have -- I will use that too during the elements of sentencing, because the Bench also asked Defence counsel if they would look at the way of sentencing and things like that in Kosovo. If we then look at the obstruction of justice, Article 309, in the disclosure we got, it was only a summary of the Article and then you would think it would be very similar to Article 77 -- sorry, Rule 77 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of the ICTY. But when you look at it carefully, and that's what I mean - anyway, the Prosecutor means that - Article 309 of the Provisional Criminal Code of Kosovo, paragraph 1, quote: "Whoever by use of force, by threat to use force or any other means of compulsion or by promise of a gift or any other form of benefit induces a witness or an expert to give a false statement in court proceedings, minor offence proceedings, administrative proceedings or in proceedings before a notary public or disciplinary proceedings shall be punished by imprisonment of six months to five years." So it's a very different criminal offence than formulated in Article -- in Rule 77. So I think that there should be some evidence that my client or anyone who is an accused in this case like this should be aware of that and this there should be some proof of that. I have also asked a lawyer in Kosovo, are there any sentencing rules, how did you -- how do the judges do that in Kosovo. And there are some general rules. He wrote me back that -- that are very similar to the rules we have here in the ICTY with mitigating and other circumstances, so that's very similar. I would like to close with some mitigating arguments, Your Honour, which would apply in the view of the Defence. The character of Beqa Beqaj as described by the Prosecution's witnesses, B1 and B2, you seldom see that the Prosecutor uses it as a [unintelligible] argument but both B1 and B2 are very sorry for the arrest of my client and would like very much for him to be back in Kosovo. The personal circumstances as described in the Defence pre-trial brief and request for provisional release, no criminal record. And his cooperation during the trial, including the conditions on provisional release, he came back for trial, like he promised to, without any guarantees from the authorities in Kosovo. Those were my closing remarks. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. van der Spoel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber has decided to deliberate and -- until Thursday. Then a hearing will be held to issue an oral decision at 5 p.m. on Thursday. The written decision will follow then as early as possible. Does the Defence or the Prosecution want to raise further issues before the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. AKERSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VAN DER SPOEL
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. The hearing stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, 5 May 2005, At 5.00 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.45 p.m.,
